doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Learning songs by ear; recording is like painting
summary: No charts; listen to the bottom and the shape. Recording is about color, and soft close-miked sounds come out big.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: How did they present the Stones or these other folks you worked with, how did they present the songs to you? Did they have a chord chart or they said here’s how it goes, sit next to you with their guitars and you just learned it that way then played your part?

Yeah. You didn’t have a part, you made up your part. Yeah. It was the old aural tradition you know. You listened to the song, sometimes somebody would just play the song and play it over and over again until you found it, you know, until you found something that you could add to it or whatever. Very improvisational. Very rarely did you even see a chord chart.

What’s the first thing you went for when you were trying to learn this song just by hearing it? I’m picturing you at a keyboard like, I think I know the answer to this, you find out what key you’re in. © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

That’s it. Listen to the bottom. Absolutely. What are we doing here? And then tried to get a sense of the shape. You know not everything is a twelve-bar blues you know. What’s the shape? What’s extended? What’s the purpose of that movement — where the chord moves right there — what’s the purpose. Is it to make it bigger? Is it to make it smaller? Is it a diversion and how can you amplify whatever the intention is. That’s sort of how I look at it, not at all in terms of the notes or harmonics but just — recording is a lot like painting I think. You’re really using colors and rhythm and stuff. And so when you first start out you think it’s about energy and jamming. But it’s not. It’s not. Because what sounds big in the real world, like turn up the volume, when you put a microphone in front of the amplifier it actually sounds smaller on tape. If you want something to sound big you make it soft and you put the microphone right up next to it and coming out of the speakers it sounds huge. So you know recording is a whole other world, frankly.
